sections.heading: When to Use Base64 and When to Avoid It
paragraphs: Base64 encoding inflates binary data by roughly thirty-three percent because every three bytes of input become four ASCII characters. This overhead is acceptable for small graphics like logos, favicons and inline UI elements, but becomes costly for large photographs or detailed illustrations.

Caching is another consideration. External image files can be cached independently by browsers and content delivery networks, so returning visitors load them from local storage without any network transfer. Base64-encoded images embedded in HTML or CSS cannot be cached separately from the document that contains them.

The sweet spot for base64 is images under roughly ten kilobytes that appear in HTML emails, single-use data URIs or situations where managing a separate file is impractical. For everything else, a hosted image with proper cache headers delivers better performance and lower bandwidth costs.

sections.heading: Small Files, Big Convenience
paragraphs: Base64 inflates data by about a third, so it suits small graphics — logos, sprites, thumbnails — rather than full-resolution photos or detailed artwork.
The resize option prepares smaller variants on the spot, giving you an email-savvy payload in the same step without opening a separate image editor.
The copied string is complete and ready to paste into your code, with no file juggling or temporary storage required.

sections.heading: Base64 in Different Programming Contexts
paragraphs: In HTML, a base64 image goes directly into an img src attribute or a CSS background-image property. The browser reads the data URI prefix, decodes the string and renders the image without requesting a single external resource.

In JavaScript, the base64 string integrates into JSON payloads, dynamic DOM construction or canvas drawing. Libraries that accept image data as strings work seamlessly with the output, enabling client-side manipulation without server round trips.

In email templates, base64 encoding bypasses the attachment-blocking behavior of many corporate mail servers. The image renders directly in the message body because it travels as text rather than as a downloadable file, improving open rates and recipient experience.

faqs.q: What exactly does base64 encoding do to my image?
faqs.a: It converts the binary image data into a text string that can be embedded in HTML, CSS or JSON, commonly with a data URI prefix and MIME type.

faqs.q: Can I resize the image before encoding?
faqs.a: Yes. An optional resize step prepares smaller, email-friendly payloads before the base64 string is generated.
Yes. Everything runs locally in your browser; the image and its string never leave your device.

faqs.q: How much larger does base64 make my image data?
faqs.a: Roughly thirty-three percent. Three bytes of binary data become four ASCII characters in the encoded string, so a ten-kilobyte image produces about thirteen kilobytes of text.

faqs.q: Can I use the output directly in an HTML email?
faqs.a: Yes. Paste the base64 string into an img src attribute with the data URI prefix. The image renders inline without requiring an external file or server hosting.
No. Base64 is an encoding, not a compression. The image data is represented as text without any modification to pixel values or visual fidelity.
